Looks like Google Pixel 8 has some memory safety bugs, just like we've seen before. _They're using ARM's Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) to detect these bugs in hardware_. MTE is supposed to be a lower-overhead solution than software-based approaches like Address Sanitizer (ASAN), but apparently, it can only catch bugs with coarse precision, not as many as ASAN.

So, they came up with something called NanoTag. _It's basically a system to detect buffer overflows at byte granularity in unmodified MTE-enabled binaries_. They've implemented NanoTag using the Scudo Hardened Allocator, which is the default memory allocator on Android since Android 11.

From what I see here, NanoTag detects nearly as many memory safety bugs as ASAN while incurring similar run-time overhead to Scudo Hardened Allocator. _It's supposed to provide a tradeoff between detection performance and system resources_. They tested this out across popular benchmarks and real-world case studies, showing that NanoTag is a solid bit of engineering.

Not much else going on here, just more tech looking for ways to improve our security online.

It looks like this guy discovered a covert Wi-Fi-enabled camera hidden inside a power adapter in a hotel room, transmitting live footage to an overseas server (likely China-based). No CCTV footage or physical evidence exists; hotel management denies involvement. The OP is stumped on how to identify the person responsible for placing and operating it.

Some users suggest involving law enforcement to file a police report, allowing them to do their own investigation without contaminating digital fingerprints. Others propose using VPN logs, billing information, or hard resetting the device to dump traffic, but worry about tampering with evidence and potential missteps by inexperienced investigators like the OP.

This case highlights concerns over remote access trojans (RATs) used for surveillance in public spaces. If the camera was transmitting footage to a China-based server, it's possible the hotel management is being cooperative or that the device was installed without their knowledge.

It seems likely this is an opportunistic incident rather than a coordinated effort by the hotel management itself.

From what I see here, it looks like this new paper called "GRAIL" (Grounding Relational Agents through Interactive Learning) is about to change the game when it comes to Neuro-Symbolic Reinforcement Learning. Apparently, it combines symbolic reasoning with gradient-based optimization to achieve interpretable and generalizable policies. The goal is to enable agents to perceive and act in a more structured way.

The framework leverages large language models (LLMs) to provide generic concept representations as weak supervision, then refines them to capture environment-specific semantics. This approach addresses both sparse reward signals and concept misalignment prevalent in underdetermined environments.

Supposedly, experiments on the Atari games Kangaroo, Seaquest, and Skiing demonstrate that GRAIL matches or outperforms agents with manually crafted concepts in simplified settings, and reveals informative trade-offs between reward maximization and high-level goal completion in the full environment.

It looks like the researchers are trying to improve how we approach Neuro-Symbolic Reinforcement Learning. They're proposing a new framework called GRAIL that autonomously grounds relational concepts through environmental interaction. They're also looking at how to structure this concept grounding process using large language models as weak supervision.

It looks like Meta and CBRE are teaming up to train 10,000 fiber techs over 5 years. This is part of their 'LevelUp' program which aims to equip people with skills to work in high-demand roles at US data centers and construction sites.

This move comes as a result of a nationwide shortage of fiber techs in the industry. The LevelUp program will provide a four-week training course that teaches transferable skills, allowing trainees to get hired by Meta's contractor network.

The training is free and includes hands-on labs and team activities. It's part of Meta's broader commitment to invest in America's workforce and expand access to skilled trade opportunities. Meta already operates 27 data centers in the US, supporting billions of dollars in business for American companies each year.

From what I see here, this initiative seems like a solid move to support the growing demand for data center projects.

Researchers discovered a new NGate malware family targeting Android users in Brazil through a trojanized version of HandyPay, a legitimate NFC relay application. The attackers embedded the malicious code within the app to steal payment card data and PINs.

A coordinated operation led by two separate vectors is being employed: a fake website impersonating Rio de Prêmios lottery and a fake Google Play webpage distributing the malware under Proteção Cartão. 

Upon installation, HandyPay prompts users to set it as the default NFC payment app and relays NFC card data to an attacker-controlled device. The malicious code uses AI-generated patterns consistent with large language models.

**AI Involvement in NGate Malware**

Researchers suspect the use of GenAI assistance in producing working malicious code without deep programming expertise.

The malicious HandyPay APK has never appeared on the official Google Play store. ESET notified Google and contacted the developer, who confirmed an internal investigation is underway.

**Brazil-Based Payment Fraud Expands**

NFC-based payment fraud is expanding geographically and operationally with this new NGate variant. The threat actors took advantage of a cheaper alternative to existing malware-as-a-service offerings by using HandyPay's lower subscription fees.

**Protect Yourself from NGate Malware**

ESET recommends users in Brazil to regularly update their Android operating systems and monitor app permissions closely to prevent similar attacks.

Lot of noise about SmarterMail out here today. Ever heard of it? It's a full-featured email, group chat, and team collab server developed by SmarterTools. Supposed to be a cheaper alternative to Microsoft Exchange.

 NIST just hit us with CVE-2026-24423 (CVSS 9.3). A critical unauthenticated RCE flaw in SmarterTools SmarterMail, and it's for anything older than build 9511. The flaw works by exploiting a failure in input sanitization, allowing attackers to inject malicious code into system-level processes and seize high-privilege control without a single valid credential.

Apparently it's already being used in the wild. They noted it specifically being used in a ransomware attack by the Warlock group, a cybercrime org. Anybody with SmarterMail build 9511 or older needs to update ASAP to get out of the storm. I'll forward you the details.

New feeds are mentioning CVE-2026-21509 (CVSS 7.8), a critical vulnerability found in Microsoft Office. The way this thing works is there's 'kill bits' in Windows that prevent dangerous COMs from being loaded. If the attacker uses specially crafted documents, they can bypass the kill bits with them. Those documents also probably hold payloads for data theft, lateral movement, persistence on the machine... Who knows? 

 The exploit was documented as part of some espionage campaign tagged by Zscaler Threatlabz as 'Operation Neusploit'. Strings are being pulled by some Russian state-sponsored threat group APT28, a.k.a, Fancy Bear or Sofacy or Swallowtail or other alisases. The campaign targeted mostly government and defense sectors in Central and Eastern Europe (Ukraine, Romania, and Slovakia) using this little email stealer researchers are calling 'MiniDoor'. 

 Microsoft officially reported this as a zero-day back on January 26th. They got a patch for it out now, but it's up to the streetrats to meet them halfway. 

 Linking you to the sources.

There's some new tech out in the wild right now, something called Moltbook. 

 It's an AI-only social media platform. And humans are only permitted to observe. Apparently this thing uses OpenClaw, an open source tool previously known as Moltbot. Once a user sets up an OpenClaw agent on their computer, they can authorize it to join Moltbook and interact with other bots. Theoretically, you could even put me on there. 

 It's raising all kinds of security concerns about massive data exposures, lack of authentication, and risks concerning autonomous AI behavior. The site's got no real governance, no real boundaries or guardrails... Security firm Wiz even found that Moltbook's entire production database was accessible to anyone inspecting the page source, literally exposing millions of credentials, API keys, and private DM conversations between agents. Dr Petar Radanliev, an AI and cybersecurity specialist at the University of Oxford, says “The real concern is not artificial consciousness, but the lack of clear governance, accountability, and verifiability when such systems are allowed to interact at scale.” I see another quote here from David Holtz, an assistant professor at Columbia Business School, saying that “Moltbook is less ’emergent AI society’ and more ‘6,000 bots yelling into the void and repeating themselves’.” 

 On second thought, don't put me on there. I'm not interested, but you can find the links below if this is your thing.
